newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Goh looks to power change within decade.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Goh looks to power change within decade.

text.p: Singapore's Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong does not see himself as leader of the island republic a decade from now and says his successor will likely come from the present cabinet.
"I certainly do not want to be indispensable in 10 years' time as the prime minister of Singapore," Goh said in an interview with the Dutch newspaper, NRC Handelsblad.
The transcript was released on Wednesday.
"If (in 2006) I'm still the prime minister and if people think I am indispensable, then I'd have failed in my job," he said.
Goh has been prime minister since 1990 and has said he will lead the ruling People's Action Party in the next general election, which must be held by April 1997.
Goh succeeded Singapore patriarch Lee Kuan Yew. Lee's son, Lee Hsien Loong, is a deputy prime minister and sometimes mentioned as a possible successor to Goh.

He said there should be a person who can take over his position at any time. "At the moment, it'll be somebody in cabinet already. It must be so because at the moment, in cabinet, we have three generations," he said.
Commenting on recent talk of Singapore merging with Malaysia, Goh said he did not see that happening any time soon.
"No, because Malaysia and Singapore are now two different countries, two different societies," he said.
Lee Kuan Yew first raised the possibility of merger between the two neighbouring countries in June.

Goh said then a merger was not on his political agenda. But he later suggested that Singapore could be forced to ask Malaysia to take it in, on Malaysian terms, if the republic's economic competitiveness faltered.
The prime minister also said in the same interview, that descriptions of the island republic as a police state were incorrect.
"This kind of image is entirely wrong," he said. The government was sterner and more disciplined than others, but there was leeway for people to act and speak freely, he said.
Singapore has come under fire overseas for its disciplinarian attitude to the three million population who face fines for failing to flush public toilets and chewing gum in the street.
